last_assistant_message: You asked me to look into the lost reminder times from the issue tracker and fix them properly rather than with another workaround, and to keep the plugin file formats stable. I read the issue, the linked forum thread and the last three releases' changelogs first, to see whether this had been patched before. It had: release 3.2 added a short delay before saving the calendar, which made the race rarer on fast machines but did nothing about its cause, and the delay is still in the code. I've removed it as part of this change, since the new store makes it unnecessary.

Before changing anything I reproduced the reported problem. With the calendar window and the bed editor both open, I set a reminder time in the calendar, then renamed a bed in the editor. The reminder time was gone after a restart. Doing the same in the other order lost the bed name instead. It happens every time, not intermittently, as long as both windows have been opened since launch. Closing either window before making the second change avoids it, which matches the workaround a few people mentioned in the issue thread.

I also checked whether anything else writes those files. The backup feature reads them but never writes. The import wizard writes beds.json once, at the end, and only when no other window is open. The two plugins write their own files under plugins/, not the shared ones. So the race is between the app's own windows only.

I started by reading how settings are stored today. Every preference lives in its own JSON file under the app's data folder: layout.json, units.json, reminders.json, beds.json and a handful of smaller ones. Each screen reads its file on open and writes it back on every change, which is why two windows open at once can overwrite each other's changes. The bug report about lost reminder times is exactly that race: the calendar window and the bed editor both rewrite reminders.json from their own stale copy.

I looked at three ways to fix it. The first was a file lock around each read-modify-write. That fixes the race but keeps a dozen files with no shared schema, and the lock has to be honoured by every screen, including the two plugins that write their own files. The second was a single JSON document with a version counter and a compare-and-swap on write. That's simpler, but every write still rewrites the whole document, and the document is already over 400 KB for users with large gardens, because the planting history is in it. The third was an embedded database.

For the database I compared SQLite with Postgres. Postgres would need a server running alongside a desktop app, which is a non-starter for something people install with a double-click, so SQLite it was. It ships with Python, handles concurrent readers and serialises writers, and the planting history becomes a table we can query instead of a list we scan.

The schema has four tables: settings (key, value, updated_at), beds, plantings and reminders. Settings that were scattered over small files become rows in the settings table. Beds and plantings keep their current fields. Reminders gain an id so two windows editing different reminders no longer collide at all.

On first launch after the update, the app looks for the old JSON files. If it finds them, it imports each one inside a single transaction, so a crash halfway leaves the old files as the source of truth and the import simply runs again next time. After a successful import the old files are renamed with a .imported suffix rather than deleted, so a user can still recover them by hand if something looks wrong. A later release can delete them.

Every screen now reads and writes through a small store module instead of touching files. The bed editor and the calendar were the two that needed real changes; the others only swapped their load and save calls. The two plugins still write their own files, which I left alone because their format is part of the plugin API, and changing it would break plugins people have written.

Tests: I added tests for the import (a clean import, a partial import after a simulated crash, and an import with a malformed beds.json, which is skipped with a warning), for two stores writing the same reminder, and for two stores writing different reminders. The full suite passes, 212 tests in all, and the import of the large sample garden takes about 0.3 seconds.
Summary: migrated the settings store from JSON files to SQLite, with the old files imported on first launch.
